title: Glad at your going
hook: no one is so lucky that no one will be glad at their death, not even Marcus (Meditations 10.36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: two questions. Your line was let it be false. Which criticism did you make false today? Day six hundred twenty.

The last day at a job: the cake, the card, the kind speeches. And somewhere in the room, someone quietly relieved you're going. Maybe you never knew, and maybe that was for the best. Marcus, emperor of Rome, writes in book ten that it would be the same at his own death: someone standing by would be glad. Not because he was cruel. Just because that's how people are. Today: schoolmaster.
screen: `THE LAST DAY AT A JOB.` → `SOMEONE QUIETLY RELIEVED.` → `GLAD AT YOUR GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. No one is so fortunate, Marcus writes, that when they're dying there won't be some standing by who welcome what's happening. Second, even the good. Suppose the person was good and wise. Won't someone still say under their breath: at last we can breathe again, free of this schoolmaster? He was never harsh with any of us, but I always felt him quietly judging us. That, Marcus says, is what's said of a good man. Third, and me? Then he turns it on himself. In my case, he says, there are many more reasons people would be glad to be rid of me. Even the companions he has worked for, prayed for and cared for, he writes, will want him gone, hoping to gain something by it. It's humbling, written by a man who ruled the Roman world. Fourth, how to hold it. The point isn't bitterness. Marcus says: don't, for this reason, go away less kindly disposed toward them. Keep your own character: friendly, well-meaning, gentle. Let go easily, he says, not as if you were being torn away. So the thought is a lightness, not a wound. You aren't the center of everyone's world, even if you're good, and that's a kind of relief. If even the gentle schoolmaster can be resented, anyone can. Hold your importance lightly, and keep being kind.
screen: `SOMEONE WILL BE GLAD.` · `EVEN THE GOOD: THE SCHOOLMASTER.` · `MORE REASONS IN MY CASE.` · `LEAVE AS KIND AS EVER.` · then, large: `LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you feel important: a team, a family, a group of friends. Let yourself picture it going on without you. Someone else running the meeting. A family dinner with your chair empty. Notice whatever comes: maybe a sting, maybe something lighter. Not everything rests on you. Breathe out a little of that weight. Then picture going back in, as kind as ever. The bell holds the time.
Schoolmaster. Marcus imagines himself as the schoolmaster someone will feel relieved to see go, even though he was never harsh. Today's word.
Your line: lightly. When you feel indispensable today, remember the schoolmaster, smile, and carry your importance lightly. Day six hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this passage to loosen the sense of being indispensable, picturing life going on without them while resolving to stay kind to everyone around them.

fork.setup: you learn someone will be relieved when you leave. you're Marcus. how do you go?
options: as kind as ever, holding your importance lightly.
fork.reveal: don't go away less kindly disposed toward them, he writes; keep being friendly, well-meaning and gentle, and let go easily.

original.note: Greek: the household slave who walked a child to school and kept watch over him. Marcus imagines being called one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad thought about death.
what it means: you're not the center of everyone's world, even if you're good; let that be a lightness, and stay kind.
what a scholar hears: the word is paidagōgos, the household slave who walked a boy to school and kept him in line; Marcus imagines a good man remembered as that kind of minder.

notes: 10.36 paraphrased (Long: 'There is no man so fortunate that there shall not be by him when he is dying some who are pleased with what is going to happen... Let us at last breathe freely being relieved from this schoolmaster... but I perceived that he tacitly condemns us'), the turn to 'in my own case', and the instruction not to depart less kindly disposed, but friendly, benevolent and mild, without being torn away. Confirm.
Confirm the Greek word in 10.36 is παιδαγωγός (or a form of it).
